history.hpi: 34-week pregnant female (G2P1) with no prior seizure history. Husband reports a roughly 1-hour prodrome of severe headache and visual disturbances (spots), followed by a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately 90 seconds. Patient is now postictal, confused, and continues to report headache. No prior history of hypertension or pre-eclampsia in this or a prior pregnancy.
history.lastOralIntake: Dinner approximately 3 hours prior to onset
history.events: Husband reports patient complained of a severe headache and blurred vision for about an hour, then had a witnessed generalized convulsive seizure lasting approximately 90 seconds

scene.dispatch: 28-year-old pregnant female, seizure activity, husband on scene, residence
scene.location: Single-family home, living room, patient on the floor where she was found postictal
scene.bystanders: Husband present, witnessed the seizure, called 911 immediately
visualCues: Postictal, confused, slow to respond to questions
No incontinence or tongue trauma noted
Husband anxious, reports this has never happened before

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 28-year-old pregnant female postictal on the living room floor after a witnessed generalized seizure. She is confused, severely hypertensive, and reports a headache that preceded the event.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin flushed and diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities spontaneously, slow to follow commands
otherFindings: Severe headache reported prior to seizure

transitions.condition: Crew recognizes that any pregnant patient beyond 20 weeks who seizes is treated as eclampsia until proven otherwise, and promptly administers magnesium sulfate along with airway support and positioning.
Crew prioritizes loading for transport without first administering magnesium sulfate; without seizure prophylaxis on board, the patient seizes again en route.

phases.name: Eclampsia recognized, magnesium given
phases.description: Crew treats the seizure as eclampsia: IV access is obtained, magnesium sulfate is administered, supplemental oxygen is applied, and the patient is positioned in the left lateral position to optimize uterine perfusion.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing that a seizure in a patient beyond 20 weeks' gestation is eclampsia until proven otherwise, the crew initiates magnesium sulfate for seizure management along with airway and positioning support.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm and less diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities spontaneously, following commands more consistently
otherFindings: Positioned left lateral to optimize uterine perfusion
O2 applied via nasal cannula, target 94-98%
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I feel groggy but I'm okay, is my baby okay?"

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize new seizure at 34 weeks gestation as eclampsia until proven otherwise
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Eclampsia: Any pregnant patient who is seizing should be assumed to have eclampsia and treated as such until arrival at the hospital. Seizure in any late term pregnancy or postpartum patient.
expectedActions.rationale: Eclampsia is a life-threatening obstetric emergency that must be assumed and treated immediately, not diagnosed by exclusion.

expectedActions.shortAction: Establish IV access; administer O2 to target 94-98% saturation
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: IV fluids: NS or LR – keep continuous infusion with maximum rate of fluids to 80 mL/hr. Administer high flow oxygen as indicated.
expectedActions.rationale: IV access is needed for magnesium administration, while supplemental O2 supports maternal and fetal oxygenation.

expectedActions.shortAction: Magnesium sulfate 6 g IV over 5-10 min for seizure management
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Seizure Management: 6 g IV over 5–10 minutes or 8 g IM (4 grams in each buttock) to prevent seizure
expectedActions.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is the definitive first-line agent to stop and prevent recurrent eclamptic seizures.

expectedActions.shortAction: Position patient left lateral or manually displace uterus to the left
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patients in second or third trimester of pregnancy should be transported on left side or with uterus manually displaced to left to ensure adequate uterine perfusion.
expectedActions.rationale: Relieves aortocaval compression from the gravid uterus, improving venous return and uterine perfusion.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess deep tendon reflexes and respiratory status after magnesium bolus
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Magnesium toxicity (progression): Hypotension followed by Loss of deep tendon reflexes followed by Somnolence, slurred speech followed by Respiratory paralysis followed by Cardiac arrest
expectedActions.rationale: Early recognition of the magnesium toxicity progression prevents respiratory paralysis and arrest.

transitions.condition: Reflexes and respiratory status remain normal after the magnesium bolus; crew proceeds with the maintenance infusion, repeat vitals, and emergent transport.
The magnesium infusion continues without interval reassessment of deep tendon reflexes or respiratory status, allowing signs of magnesium toxicity to progress unrecognized.

phases.name: DTRs reassessed, transport initiated
phases.description: With reflexes and respiratory status confirmed normal, the crew continues the magnesium infusion, treats persistent severe hypertension, and initiates emergent transport with serial vital signs.
phases.triggerCondition: After confirming intact deep tendon reflexes and stable respirations following the magnesium bolus, the crew continues the maintenance infusion, addresses persistent severe hypertension, and transports emergently.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, skin warm and dry
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Deep tendon reflexes intact, moves all extremities normally
otherFindings: Magnesium infusion continuing at maintenance rate
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "My headache is a little better now."

expectedActions.shortAction: Repeat blood pressure and vital signs every 10 minutes during transport
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Monitoring: Vital signs including repeat blood pressures every 10 min. Reassess vital signs every 10 minutes during transport.
expectedActions.rationale: Frequent reassessment detects both recurrent severe hypertension and evolving magnesium toxicity.

expectedActions.shortAction: Continue magnesium sulfate maintenance infusion at 2 g/hr
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Magnesium sulfate: 4 g IV over 5–10 min, followed by 2 g/hr
expectedActions.rationale: Ongoing infusion maintains therapeutic magnesium levels to prevent seizure recurrence.

expectedActions.shortAction: Labetalol 20 mg IV over 2 minutes for persistent severe hypertension
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Severe hypertension (SBP greater than 160 or DBP greater than 110) lasting more than 15 min with associated preeclampsia symptoms... Labetalol 20 mg IV over 2 minutes. May repeat every 10 minutes X 2 doses for persistent severe hypertension with preeclampsia symptoms. Ensure that HR is greater than 60 BPM prior to administration.
expectedActions.rationale: Sustained severe hypertension with preeclampsia symptoms carries a maternal stroke risk and requires treatment toward a goal BP of roughly 140/90.

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport emergently to closest appropriate receiving facility; notify en route
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Disposition: Transport emergently to closest appropriate receiving facility – notify en route if possible so the receiving team can prepare
expectedActions.rationale: Definitive management of eclampsia requires obstetric facility resources and delivery capability.

phases.name: Magnesium delayed, transport prioritized
phases.description: Without magnesium sulfate on board, seizure prophylaxis is absent during transport. The patient has a second generalized convulsive seizure en route.
phases.triggerCondition: The crew loads and begins transport without first administering magnesium sulfate; roughly ten minutes later, the patient has a second witnessed generalized seizure in the moving ambulance.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Compromised by active convulsive movement, oral secretions
otherFindings: Fetal heart tones not assessable during active convulsion
Crew unable to safely reassess blood pressure during seizure

expectedActions.shortAction: Midazolam 4 mg IV (78 kg x 0.1 mg/kg = 7.8 mg -> cap at 4 mg max) for recurrent seizure
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If vascular access (IV or IO) is present: ... Midazolam 0.1 mg/kg IV or IO, maximum 4 mg. Benzodiazepine, per Seizures Guideline, for active seizure not responding to magnesium. Caution: respiratory depression
expectedActions.rationale: A recurrent eclamptic seizure not immediately covered by magnesium requires rescue benzodiazepine, with caution for added respiratory depression.

phases.name: DTRs not reassessed
phases.description: The magnesium infusion continues unchecked. Deep tendon reflexes are lost, the patient becomes increasingly somnolent, and respirations slow — early signs of magnesium toxicity progressing toward respiratory paralysis.
phases.triggerCondition: Without interval reassessment of reflexes or respiratory status, the magnesium infusion continues at maintenance rate while toxicity signs progress: hypotension, loss of deep tendon reflexes, and somnolence with slowed respirations.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but at risk, diminished gag response
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Deep tendon reflexes absent, diminished response to painful stimuli
otherFindings: No deep tendon reflexes elicited at patellar tendon

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize absent DTRs, somnolence, and slurred speech as magnesium toxicity
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Magnesium toxicity (progression): Hypotension followed by Loss of deep tendon reflexes followed by Somnolence, slurred speech followed by Respiratory paralysis followed by Cardiac arrest
expectedActions.rationale: Recognizing the toxicity progression before respiratory paralysis develops allows for reversal before arrest.

expectedActions.shortAction: Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion immediately
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Treatment of magnesium toxicity: Stop magnesium drip
expectedActions.rationale: Halting the infusion prevents further accumulation and worsening toxicity.

expectedActions.shortAction: Calcium gluconate 3 g IV to reverse magnesium toxicity; support respirations
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Give calcium gluconate 3 g IV or calcium chloride 1 g IV in cases of pending respiratory arrest. Support respiratory effort.
expectedActions.rationale: Calcium directly antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction, reversing toxicity before respiratory paralysis occurs.
